verses.3: Magnify your Lord, purify your garment, and avoid impurity.
verses.4: Al-Mizan records six readings of purifying the garment: refining actions, which it finds plausible because outward conduct covers inward belief; cleansing the soul from sin; shortening a dress to keep it from impurity; keeping one’s spouse from disbelief and sin, since spouses are a garment (2:187); acquiring virtues; and literally cleansing clothing as a condition of ṣalāh. On the literal reading, this verse and the preceding takbīr prescribe prayer at the beginning of the mission. The objection that prayer was not yet legislated fails, because ṣalāh was obligatory from the outset, although the five daily prayers were fixed at the miʿrāj, first as ten units and then with seven added. The first and literal readings are judged most plausible.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan gives three readings of al-rujz: punishment, hence avoiding the sin that causes it; every evil act or trait disliked by God, perhaps vices after deeds have been covered by the preceding verse; or idols. It reads mann in (74:6) contextually as the hurtful reminder of one’s favour, illustrated by (2:264) and (49:17), and istikthār as considering something great rather than seeking abundance. The command therefore forbids treating obedience to the preceding injunctions as a great personal favour: a servant possesses and controls only what God grants under His authority, and must comply with His command.

Other interpretations—giving for a larger return, seeking payment or gratitude for the prophetic message, treating one’s service or charity as a favour, awaiting reward for charity, or prohibiting a loan that demands ribā—are listed as less commensurate with the context; the translator notes that the patience-to-reward clause belongs to the next verse. “Be patient for your Lord” means for His satisfaction and includes patience through affliction and abuse while warning, perseverance in obedience, and restraint from sin; it consequently encompasses patience in itself, against polytheist abuse, and in fulfilling obligations.
verses.6: Do not regard your favour as great.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan presents this Meccan sūrah of fifty-six verses as among the earliest revelations: it commands the Prophet’s patience and warning, exalts the Qur’an, and threatens those who call it sorcery and turn from it. Reports that it, or its opening seven verses, was the first revelation conflict with its context; the opening of Sūrah al-ʿAlaq appears more likely. Its being the first sūrah revealed for the public call can reconcile differing reports, but remains only possible.

Al-Mizan reads al-muddaththir, originally mutadaththir from tadaththur, as one wrapped in a garment for sleep: the Prophet was in that state, and the affectionate title derives from it. Prophethood as a garment, seclusion in Ḥirāʾ, and leisure ending for the work of guidance are possible readings, but the contextual sense comes first. “Rise and warn” is an unrestricted command to undertake warning, possibly addressed to kin or to all humanity; glad tidings are unmentioned because warning suited this initial stage.

The commentary takes fa-kabbir, from takbīr, to require magnifying God in belief, speech, and practice: He has no equal, superior, partner, defect, or defining attribute. A narration from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt explains takbīr as God’s being greater than every description. Unlike tasbīḥ, which removes defect-implying attributes, takbīr places Him beyond every bounded attribute whatsoever. The verse may also concern the opening Allāh akbar of prayer, while its fāʾ can mean to continue magnifying Him in every circumstance.

verses.28: It spares nothing and leaves nothing.
verses.31: Al-Mizan treats verses 8–31 as a severe warning to those who deride the Qur’an as sorcery. Naqr is striking, and the nāqūr is an instrument struck to sound, like blowing the ṣūr: it signifies resurrection and summons to judgment. Two construals of yawmaʾidh—either the day of return or the time of the trumpet’s sounding on that day—have effectively the same result: a day hard in every respect for disbelievers. Multiple narrations connect the following threat to Walīd b. al-Mughīrah. The preferred reading of waḥīdan is that God alone, without help, created and perfectly directed him; readings that it means leaving God alone with him, that Walīd was created destitute, or an omitted command to criticize are alternatives. God gave him abundant or ever-increasing wealth, sons at hand, and provision, yet he demanded more and proudly opposed the signs; ṣaʿūd depicts the forced, painful ascent of his punishment. His reflection and appraisal arrange possible accusations—poetry, soothsaying, madness, or myth—against the Qur’an until he chooses inherited magic and human speech, allegedly because it divides a person from family and friends. The repeated curse answers this calculation. Looking, frowning, and scowling form an eloquent visible sequence; his inward arrogant turning away is then disclosed in that utterance. Saqar, a name or level of hell, clarifies the threatened hardship. It burns all that reaches it and every aspect of those cast into it, unlike worldly fire; alternatively, it neither leaves them alive nor lets them die. Readings about recurrent re-creation or leaving neither flesh nor bone are also reported. Lawwāḥah blackens, or possibly reddens, the outer skin. The nineteen are guards; their being angels is established by the next verse, not by an anecdote in which Abū Jahl and Abū al-Ashadd call each keeper a man. Al-Mizan explains that the guards are angels able to execute God’s command, so sinners cannot resist them as they might humans. Announcing their number is fitnah, a test for the faithless, while its accord with earlier scripture reassures the People of the Book and increases believers’ faith. The lām of that reassurance states a divine purpose; the lām concerning diseased hearts and faithless mockers asking what God means states an eventual consequence. Their question scorns the nineteen as too few to punish jinn and humankind; disease denotes doubt and denial, often matched with hypocrisy. God’s hosts are angels whose reality, qualities, number, acts, and creative wisdom are known only to Him, so none may disparage them as few. The statement of nineteen is an admonition for all humanity, supporting the universality of the Qur’an’s teaching; proposed antecedents for “it” include the hosts, Saqar, the whole sūrah, and worldly fire, the last being least plausible. The commentary rejects the claim that mentioning hypocrites makes this Meccan sūrah a miraculous prediction of a later Medinan phenomenon. Muqātil’s reported assignment of (74:31) to Medina is questionable and only inferred from that assumption. Hypocrisy can arise from long-term gain, tribal bigotry, or ingrained polytheist conditioning, not only fear or immediate advantage; nothing proves these absent in Mecca. It notes accounts of early doubters and apostates and finds Meccan (29:10-11) explicitly concerned with hypocrisy amid persecution. Although (22:11) is Medinan, it describes the same unstable attitude.

verses.48: Al-Mizan says these verses refute the prior charge of sorcery: the Qur’an is among God’s greatest communications, warning all humanity, and adherence to it frees the soul from the bondage of deeds that lead to hell. Kallā may qualify the warning’s effect on those who refuse it, or deny that the Qur’an is one of the greatest signs; the night’s recession and the dawn’s brightness are oaths. Although many exegetes take “it” in (74:35) as Saqar, the commentary finds the Qur’an more plausible, because Walīd’s accusation and the sūrah’s close focus on it. It is a great warning; readings that make it the Prophet or God are not worth pursuing. “Advance” means following truth in faith and obedience, and “retreat” refusing it in disbelief and disobedience; an alternative reverses the grammatical order and takes them as hastening to, or declining, good works. Every soul is rahīnah, a pledge or hostage for what it earns. The bāʾ may mean accompaniment, causation, or reciprocity; Al-Mizan insists that rahīnah is a noun synonymous with rahn, not a feminine adjective. Each soul is held to God until it pays His due through faith and righteous deeds, then freed; one who dies in disbelief and sin remains confined. This differs from (52:21), where being hostage means deeds are inseparable from their doer. The People of the Right Hand are ordinary believers with true beliefs and righteous acts who receive their records from the right and are released into incomparable gardens. The al-sābiqūn and al-muqarrabūn are a third class, already at perfect servitude, possessing neither souls nor acts independently and therefore not summoned to account (56:7-11) and (37:127-128); readings that identify the People of the Right Hand with angels, deceased Muslim children, covenantal people, or those promised reward are rejected as implausible. The garden dwellers question the guilty about entering Saqar. The guilty as a group lacked ṣalāh, the worshipful turning to God in any divine law; failed to feed the poor, the people’s right alongside prayer as God’s right; immersed themselves in improper speech or conduct; and denied the Day of Retribution. The collective wording need not mean every individual had every vice. Al-yaqīn may mean death, which ended their lifelong denial, or the certainty encountered through the hereafter’s signs and barzakh at and after death. Intercessors do exist, but these guilty people receive no benefit because they do not meet intercession’s conditions.
verses.49: Al-Mizan likens their aversion to the Reminder to terrified asses fleeing a lion.

verses.56:
Al-Mizan says these verses conclude the warnings by expressing astonishment that people evade so plain a Qur’anic reminder. They may accept or reject it, but their choice is not independent of God’s qadar. The rhetorical question asks what has happened to the polytheists who ought to confirm the message but flee it; they are like wild asses stampeding from a lion or hunter.

Their demand for individually unrolled scriptures is not mere panic but arrogant refusal of a true, manifestly supported call brought by a human messenger. The verse requires a separate divine book for each person, unlike the single book demanded in (17:93); demands for named commands to believe or guarantees of bounty and immunity from punishment are incongruent with the context. The demand is unnecessary because clear proofs complete God’s case against the messenger and all people, while messengership needs a purity and spiritual preparation others lack. Its real motive is fearlessness of the hereafter: if they feared it, they would believe once proof was complete rather than demand another miracle.

The Qur’an itself is the sufficient reminder, with the recompense of obedience and disobedience preserved by God. Whoever wills may heed it in the sphere of uncoerced choice. Yet voluntary remembrance remains subject to God’s creational, causal irādah takwīniyyah: God has ordained that a person acts through choice, so the act is contingent on that person while still dependent on divine decree; without that will it would not occur. God is worthy of Godwariness through His absolute sovereignty over happiness and wretchedness, and worthy to forgive those who fear Him through His forgiveness and mercy. These attributes justify both the call to remember and the assertion of God’s prevailing decree; no one can defeat His will through defiance.
